items.take: Barr's Nov. 18 speech highlighted Syracuse, New York, which announced earlier this year a revolving loan fund for mixed-income housing. items.headline: Barr: 44% of Americans live in low-income communities; most households hold little wealth
items.take: In a Nov. 18 speech, Fed Governor Michael Barr cited recent estimates that 44 percent of Americans live in low-income communities, where a fifth or more of people live below the poverty line. He said the Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that the majority of households has very little wealth, and that lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help. items.headline: BoE market group: energy prices and market rates correlated; views split on shock effects
items.take: According to the MPG minutes, participants noted the correlation between energy prices and market rates and how it has evolved over recent months. items.headline: BoE market group flags AI debt financing, hedge-fund leverage, sovereign and cyber risks
items.take: The Bank of England's MPG minutes say participants noted the support to global growth from AI-related capital expenditure and discussed the increasing role of debt financing, plus the implications of a change in AI expectations for risky asset markets. They also covered potential vulnerabilities from elevated hedge-fund leverage, sovereign debt pressures and cyber risks. items.headline: BoE market group: UK growth resilience 'strengthened the case for higher rates'
items.take: Minutes of the Bank of England's Market Participants Group meeting of Nov. 18, published Nov. 19, say participants noted the resilience of UK growth this year despite the energy shock. items.take: The minutes of the Oct. 27-28 meeting say the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, approved by a 10-2 vote. Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voted against, preferring to raise the target range by 1/4 percentage point at that meeting. items.headline: FOMC minutes: almost all participants saw a further rate increase as likely appropriate
items.take: The minutes say almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective. Most participants expressed support for maintaining the range at the October meeting. AlphaGen read: the minutes point to a Committee debating when to raise rates, not whether.

items.headline: FOMC minutes: some wanted 25 bp in October; a couple floated more than 25 bp next

items.headline: EIA explains how it reconciles energy supply and demand: stock change plus other
items.take: EIA's Monthly Energy Review defines supply as production plus imports and demand as consumption plus exports, with demand minus supply equal to stock change plus other. Stock change is the net difference between energy in storage at the start and end of a month. AlphaGen read: the monthly balance is closed by this accounting line, so small revisions can show up there.

The Japanese yen was at 159.93 per dollar on Nov. 13, up from 157.76 on Nov. 5, a 2.17-yen move in the dollar's favor. AlphaGen read: both pairs moved toward a firmer dollar over the same eight days in which the 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.84% to 5.15%.
items.source_name: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System via FRED (DEXUSEU)

items.headline: Fed balance sheet $6.759T on Nov. 11, up $10.7B from the prior week
items.take: FRED shows Federal Reserve total assets (WALCL) at $6,758,867 million on Nov. 11, up $10,722 million from $6,748,145 million on Nov. 4. Weekly levels were $6,747,560 million on Oct. 7 and $6,755,639 million on Oct. 14, so the balance sheet has stayed in a narrow band since early October. AlphaGen read: the six weekly readings since Oct. 7 span $13.2 billion, and this week's $10.7 billion gain is the largest of the five weekly changes.
items.source_name: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System via FRED (WALCL)

items.headline: Diamondback agrees to buy Double Eagle subsidiaries for 15.56M shares plus $2.15B cash
items.take: Diamondback announced a definitive agreement on Nov. 16 to acquire certain subsidiaries of Double Eagle IV Midco and Double Eagle V Midco for about 15.56 million shares of common stock and $2.15 billion of cash, subject to customary adjustments. The company says the assets cover about 176,000 net acres in the Midland Basin and expects closing on Dec. 21, 2026. AlphaGen read: Diamondback describes it as buying out the 40% of the partnership it did not already own, so this consolidates an existing stake rather than opening a new position.
items.source_name: Diamondback Energy, Inc. (Form 8-K, Exhibit 99.1)

items.headline: Aon completes its acquisition of USI for a total purchase price of $17.0B
items.take: Aon plc said on Nov. 16 it completed the acquisition of USI for a total purchase price of $17.0 billion. Aon describes USI as the tenth largest U.S. insurance broker, with about $3 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,500 team members, and cites $395 million of expected net adjusted EBITDA synergies. AlphaGen read: Aon will update its 2027 outlook, including USI, when it reports fourth-quarter earnings in early 2027.
items.source_name: Aon plc (Form 8-K, Exhibit 99.1)

items.headline: Moderna cuts term-loan margins 0.75 point and extends maturity to Nov. 24, 2031
items.take: In an 8-K filed Nov. 16, Moderna disclosed Amendment No. 1 to its November 2025 credit agreement with Ares Capital as administrative agent, effective Nov. 9. Margins fall from 5.50% to 4.75% on SOFR-based loans and from 4.50% to 3.75% on base-rate loans, and maturity moves from Nov. 24, 2030 to Nov. 24, 2031. AlphaGen read: the delayed-draw availability periods are also extended to Nov. 24, 2029, which keeps those commitments open longer.
items.source_name: Moderna, Inc. (Form 8-K, Item 1.01)

items.headline: Keurig Dr Pepper starts a $2.0B common stock offering to repay about $2.0B of debt
items.take: KDP's Nov. 12 release, furnished in an 8-K filed Nov. 16, says it commenced an underwritten public offering of $2.0 billion of common stock, with a 30-day underwriter option for up to $300 million more. It intends to use net proceeds to repay or repurchase about $2.0 billion of debt ahead of its planned separation into Beverage Co. and Global Coffee Co., targeted for early 2027. AlphaGen read: the stated aim is to strengthen the investment-grade profile of both companies after the split.
items.source_name: Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. (Form 8-K, Exhibit 99.1)

items.headline: Cheniere promotes Zach Davis to President and Chief Financial Officer
items.take: Cheniere announced on Nov. 16 that Zach Davis was promoted to President and CFO from Executive Vice President and CFO, effective Nov. 12, 2026. He has been CFO since August 2020 and continues to report to Chairman and CEO Jack Fusco. AlphaGen read: this is a title and scope change for an existing executive, not a change of CFO.
items.source_name: Cheniere Energy, Inc. (Form 8-K, Exhibit 99.1)

items.headline: 10-year breakeven 2.20% on Nov. 16 while the 10-2 spread widened to 0.29 point
items.take: FRED shows the 10-year breakeven inflation rate at 2.20% on Nov. 16, down from 2.24% on Nov. 13, and the 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread at 0.29 percentage point, up from 0.27 on Nov. 13. The spread was 0.35 on Nov. 6 and 0.32 on Nov. 9 in the same series. AlphaGen read: breakevens eased while the curve steepened slightly, so the Nov. 16 moves do not point to a fresh inflation-expectations shock.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED), T10YIE and T10Y2Y

items.headline: PPI final demand: ten 2026 monthly changes compound to about 5.7%
items.take: BLS's October PPI release shows final demand changes of +0.6, +0.5, +0.8, +1.1, +0.5, -0.1, +0.1, +0.4, +1.4 and +0.3 percent for January through October, with June the only decline. Compounding those published, rounded figures gives roughly 5.7% over the ten months, against a 12-month change of 6.5% for the period ended in October. AlphaGen read: March (+0.8%), April (+1.1%) and September (+1.4%) were the three largest monthly gains, so the cumulative figure is driven by a few large months rather than a steady drift.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: PPI final demand energy: four declines in 2026, but monthly changes compound to ~34%
items.take: BLS's October PPI table shows final demand energy changing -1.7, +2.0, +10.5, +7.1, +8.2, -7.2, -1.5, +4.2, +10.0 and -0.1 percent from January through October. Four of the ten months were declines, and six were gains of 2.0% or more. Compounding the published, rounded monthly figures gives roughly 34.4% over the ten months. AlphaGen read: March (+10.5%) and September (+10.0%) were the two largest monthly moves, which dominates the compounded total.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: PPI transportation and warehousing services: six of ten 2026 months rose 2% or more
items.take: In BLS's October PPI table, final demand transportation and warehousing services changed +1.0, +0.8, +2.2, +3.7, +2.1, -0.3, -1.1, +2.4, +3.4 and +2.0 percent from January through October. Six months were gains of 2.0% or more and two were declines (June and July). Compounding the published, rounded figures gives roughly 17.3% over the ten months. AlphaGen read: October's +2.0% is the third straight gain of that size after the June-July dip.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: PPI final demand foods rose 1.3% in October, the largest monthly gain since February
items.take: BLS's October PPI table shows final demand foods up 1.3% in October after +1.1% in September, versus +2.3% in February; the other seven 2026 months ranged from -1.3% to +0.6%. Five of the ten months were declines, and compounding the published, rounded changes gives roughly +2.0% for January through October. AlphaGen read: foods compounded to about 2.0% against about 34.4% for energy, though the last two months have turned upward.
items.source_name: BLS, Producer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: 8-week bill high rate 4.132% on Oct. 15, up 7.2 bp from 4.060% on Oct. 8
items.take: Treasury results show the $105 billion 8-week bill auctioned Oct. 15 had a 4.132% high investment rate and a 2.26 bid-to-cover ratio, versus 4.060% and 2.77 on Oct. 8. Indirect bidders were accepted for $47.89 billion of $112.08 billion total accepted on Oct. 15, against $71.40 billion of $113.92 billion a week earlier. AlphaGen read: unlike the 4-week bill, whose bid-to-cover rose over the same week, the 8-week saw coverage fall as its rate increased.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: 17-week bill high rate 4.313% on Oct. 14 with a 2.79 bid-to-cover, the highest in the latest results
items.take: Treasury results show the $75 billion 17-week bill auctioned Oct. 14 had a 4.313% high investment rate and a 2.79 bid-to-cover ratio, with $80.05 billion total accepted. Among the eight bill auctions in the latest results, 2.79 was the highest bid-to-cover; the 8-week on Oct. 15 had the lowest at 2.26. AlphaGen read: the 17-week had the strongest coverage of the six bill maturities in these results.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: 26-week bill cleared 16.6 bp above the 13-week on Oct. 13: 4.351% vs 4.185%
items.take: Treasury results show the $95 billion 13-week bill auctioned Oct. 13 had a 4.185% high investment rate and a 2.68 bid-to-cover, while the $82 billion 26-week bill had 4.351% and 2.76. The 16.6 basis-point gap is computed from the two stated rates. AlphaGen read: the 26-week offered a modestly higher rate for the longer maturity at that day's auctions.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: Treasury bill offerings Oct. 13-15 ranged from $75B (17-week) to $110B (4-week)
items.take: Treasury's latest auction results list offering amounts of $110 billion for the 4-week, $95 billion each for the 6-week and 13-week, $105 billion for the 8-week, $75 billion for the 17-week and $82 billion for the 26-week. Total accepted exceeded the offering amount in each case, from $80.05 billion for the 17-week to $117.41 billion for the 4-week. AlphaGen read: the 4-week and 8-week sizes together total $215 billion of the six offerings listed.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: Primary dealers took 27% of the Oct. 15 4-week bill, vs 31% on Oct. 8
items.take: Treasury results show primary dealers were accepted for $31.67 billion of $117.41 billion total accepted in the 4-week bill auction on Oct. 15, about 27.0%, versus $37.49 billion of $119.35 billion, about 31.4%, on Oct. 8. Indirect bidders rose to $64.87 billion from $58.73 billion. AlphaGen read: indirect bidders accounted for more of the 4-week bill accepted amount in the latest auction than a week earlier.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: BEA: Q3 inventory build led by wholesale trade and manufacturing, nondurable goods
items.take: BEA said the increase in Q3 investment primarily reflected private inventory investment and equipment. The largest contributors to inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing, both led by nondurable goods industries, based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data. AlphaGen read: inventories and equipment are the two named drivers of the Q3 investment increase behind 3.4% real GDP growth at an annual rate; BEA's second estimate is due Nov. 25.
items.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis

items.headline: September: personal income +0.2% while PCE prices rose 0.5%, versus +0.3% each in August
items.take: BEA's table shows current-dollar personal income rose 0.2% in September after 0.3% in August, while the PCE price index rose 0.5% after 0.3%. Real disposable personal income fell 0.3% in September after no change in August. AlphaGen read: prices outran income growth in the month, which is the arithmetic behind the decline in real disposable income.
items.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis

items.headline: Payrolls: Aug-Oct gains average 137,000 after revisions, using 186,000, 60,000 and 165,000
items.take: After BLS revised August to +186,000 and September to +60,000, and reported October at +165,000, the three months total 411,000, an average of 137,000 a month (AlphaGen calculation). BLS said August and September combined are 84,000 higher than previously reported. AlphaGen read: the three-month average is well above the 48,000 average monthly gain BLS cites for the prior 12 months.
items.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics

items.headline: Average hourly earnings rose 14 cents to $38.00 in October, up 3.1% in 12 months
items.take: BLS reported average hourly earnings for all private nonfarm employees rose 14 cents, or 0.4%, to $38.00 in October, and are up 3.1% over the past 12 months. For production and nonsupervisory employees, hourly earnings rose 12 cents, or 0.4%, to $32.75. AlphaGen read: pay growth of 3.1% over 12 months sits below the 3.6% 12-month September PCE inflation rate BEA reported, though the two series cover different months.
items.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics

items.headline: ECB's Vujčić: IPO volumes on track to exceed dot-com high relative to U.S. GDP
items.take: In his Nov. 16 Euro Finance Week speech, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić said equity issuance is surging, with IPO volumes now on track to exceed the dot-com bubble high relative to U.S. GDP. He added that such surges have historically often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism. AlphaGen read: the ECB is treating issuance volume itself, not just valuations, as a stability signal.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: ECB publishes its Financial Stability Review two days after Nov. 16 speech
items.take: Vujčić said the ECB publishes its latest Financial Stability Review two days after his Nov. 16 remarks, and that an early-release special feature on AI-related cyber capabilities and concentration of ICT third-party providers was published that day. He named AI and sovereign debt markets as the two risks that stand out most versus a year ago. AlphaGen read: the full review lands this week and should expand on both themes.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: euro-area underlying inflation stable, wages not responding materially yet
items.take: Vujčić said euro-area headline inflation rose to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, mainly on energy, while underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. He said weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain the energy-driven rise by weighing on growth. AlphaGen read: the ECB is separating an energy shock from broader price-setting.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić flags leveraged hedge funds in sovereign bond markets, Japanese investor risk
items.take: Vujčić said hedge funds have become a significant but procyclical source of liquidity in sovereign bond markets, and that large Japanese investors may further reduce euro-area government bond holdings if Japanese yields rise. He said the growing footprint of leveraged hedge funds creates additional vulnerabilities. AlphaGen read: the ECB sees the buyer base for sovereign debt as increasingly price-sensitive.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Warsh: research effort up 20x+ since the 1930s, yet research productivity fell more
items.take: Opening the Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference on Nov. 16, Chairman Warsh cited estimates that research efforts have increased more than 20 times since the 1930s, while, quoting Bloom, Jones and coauthors, research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount. He said productivity growth has been reasonably strong in recent quarters but has not broken out definitively to the upside. AlphaGen read: the Chair is framing the AI debate around idea generation, not just capital spending.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: 4-week bill high rate 4.068% on Oct. 15, up 2.0 bp from 4.048% a week earlier
items.take: Treasury results show the $110 billion 4-week bill auctioned Oct. 15 had a 4.068% high investment rate and a 2.56 bid-to-cover ratio, versus 4.048% and 2.40 for the $110 billion offering on Oct. 8. The 8-week bill on Oct. 15 cleared at 4.132% with a 2.26 bid-to-cover. AlphaGen read: demand at the front end firmed slightly for the 4-week even as the rate edged up.
items.source_name: U.S. Treasury, Fiscal Data auctions

items.headline: Elderson: ECB aims to cut small banks' reporting to about 5% of large banks' data points
items.take: In a Nov. 16 opinion piece, the ECB's Frank Elderson said the ECB and the European Banking Authority are pursuing reforms that should ultimately reduce reporting by small and non-complex banks to around 5% of the data points reported by large banks. He said supervisors could also run stress-test projections centrally, lightening the workload for almost 1,000 institutions, while stressing that proportionality cannot mean lower standards. AlphaGen read: the ECB is pairing simpler reporting with an explicit safety-and-soundness caveat.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Barr flags fast chip depreciation risk; older-vintage lease rates 'holding up'
items.take: Governor Barr said the bulk of a data center's cost comes from GPUs and other specialized chips, and one concern is that they may depreciate quickly as newer technologies overtake them, leaving capacity of little future use. He said lease rates of older chip vintages currently appear to be holding up, suggesting uses even for older computing technology. AlphaGen read: collateral values of GPU-backed financings depend on how long older chips stay in demand.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: equity-strategy leverage has risen, with prime brokers at large dealers a channel
items.take: Governor Barr said leverage at hedge funds and risk appetite appear quite high, so a sharp reversal could lead to rapid deleveraging and self-reinforcing fire sales, and that leverage used in equity strategies has also increased in recent years, provided in part via large dealers' prime brokerage. He said high capital at the largest banks is a bulwark against spillovers but counterparty exposures could rise in a period of equity-market volatility. AlphaGen read: the Fed's concern centers on the leveraged-fund channel rather than direct AI-related losses.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: equity premium low versus history, though not as low as the dot-com peak
items.take: Governor Barr said the equity premium, a rough measure of the extra return investors require for holding stocks over risk-free bonds, is at low levels relative to historical norms, though not nearly as low as in the dot-com boom. He noted the Fed does not target financial-market levels and called the premium one indicator among several of valuations. AlphaGen read: the Fed is framing valuations as a financial-stability input, not a market call.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: hyperscaler capex and debt yet to surpass the 1990s telecom cycle, but may soon
items.take: Governor Barr said the Fed's Financial Stability Report compares hyperscalers' cumulative capital spending and debt issuance since 2020 with those of all telecommunications firms during the broadband cycle that began in 1995. He said hyperscalers have yet to surpass their comparators, but the recent acceleration in capital expenditures suggests they may do so soon. AlphaGen read: the Fed is using the telecom buildout as its reference case for a debt-funded technology cycle.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Barr: Fed's FSR puts hyperscaler off-balance-sheet obligations above $3 trillion
items.take: In his Nov. 16 Milan speech, Fed Governor Barr said the Financial Stability Report estimates the potential maximum nominal value of hyperscalers' long-term contracts, lease commitments and residual value guarantees now exceeds $3 trillion. He said these have grown even more rapidly than on-balance-sheet debt and that the opacity of such structures can exacerbate selloffs, so they warrant close monitoring. AlphaGen read: the Fed is flagging contingent AI-related commitments, not just reported debt, as the place risk could hide.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Vujčić: sovereign debt fragilities rising on both sides of the Atlantic
items.take: In his Nov. 16 Euro Finance Week keynote, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić said sovereign debt fragilities have further increased on both sides of the Atlantic and are among the factors driving up long-term yields. He said hedge funds have become a significant but procyclical source of liquidity, and that large Japanese investors may further reduce euro area government bond holdings if Japanese yields rise. AlphaGen read: the ECB is linking bond-market supply and investor-base shifts to financial stability.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić asks if AI debt issuance could crowd out other borrowers
items.take: Vujčić said the substantial financing needs of the AI investment boom raise questions about competition for capital between public and private borrowers, including whether AI-related debt issuance could put upward pressure on financing costs or crowd out other investment. He also said firms are increasingly relying on opaque off-balance-sheet financing structures and circular financial arrangements. AlphaGen read: the ECB is treating AI funding as a credit-market issue, not only an equity one.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: private credit's rapid growth warrants close monitoring
items.take: Vujčić said private credit can diversify financing sources for firms and that risks currently appear contained, but its rapid growth warrants close monitoring given limited transparency, growing interconnectedness with banks and insurers, and potential liquidity mismatches. He said tools to address systemic risks in the non-bank sector remain limited compared with banking. AlphaGen read: the ECB is pressing for a system-wide framework for non-bank finance.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Vujčić: euro-area bank capital buffers not a binding lending constraint
items.take: Vujčić said euro-area banks have maintained strong capital and liquidity positions, supported by solid profitability and retained earnings, and that current regulatory capital buffers do not appear to be a binding constraint on lending. He said they should be preserved as insurance against future shocks. He added that the Financial Stability Review is due two days after the speech. AlphaGen read: the ECB is signaling no appetite to loosen buffers.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Elderson: ECB backs raising small-bank threshold to €10bn, adding about 150 banks
items.take: ECB Executive Board member Frank Elderson wrote on Nov. 16 that the small and non-complex bank framework requires a balance sheet below €5 billion today, and that amending the regulation to let national authorities raise it to €10 billion would, with a redefinition of non-complex, bring about 150 more banks under it. He said joint reforms with the EBA should ultimately reduce reporting by such banks to around 5% of the data points reported by large banks. AlphaGen read: this is a proposal, and he stressed that proportionality cannot mean lower standards.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread 0.27 point on Nov. 13, from 0.38 on Nov. 5
items.take: FRED shows the 10-year minus 2-year Treasury constant-maturity spread at 0.27 percentage point on Nov. 13, up 0.03 from 0.24 on Nov. 12 and down 0.11 from 0.38 on Nov. 5. AlphaGen read: the curve is still positively sloped but flatter than at the start of the month.
items.source_name: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

items.headline: Warsh calls "super intelligence" a general-purpose technology that demands Fed attention
items.take: Opening the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco, Chairman Warsh called the arrival of "super intelligence" an "entirely new force in economic life and society." He said the Fed's role is "neither advocacy nor opposition," but that wide adoption will have significant impact on the economy, with implications for monetary policy "down the road." AlphaGen read: the Chairman is framing AI as a policy input to plan for, not a call on rates.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh: productivity growth "reasonably strong" lately but no definitive breakout yet
items.take: Chairman Warsh said productivity growth has fluctuated and, in recent quarters, "it's been reasonably strong," but "it hasn't yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside." He cited Bloom, Jones and coauthors: research efforts have increased more than 20 times since the 1930s, yet research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount. AlphaGen read: the Chairman did not claim an AI productivity boom is yet visible in the data.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh outlines three illustrative AI scenarios Fed staff are modeling, "not forecasts"
items.take: Chairman Warsh said Board staff have begun evaluating contingencies with stylized, model-based frameworks: broadly shared gains with real GDP growth persistently above its long-run average; labor market disruption that could push the jobless rate above levels consistent with full employment; or a disappointment in which equity valuations fall, bringing a slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment. He called them "illustrative scenarios, not forecasts." AlphaGen read: the spread of outcomes shows why the Fed describes this as planning rather than predicting.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh: Productivity and Jobs panel is one of five task forces he has convened
items.take: Chairman Warsh said the Productivity and Jobs Task Force is "one of five" he has convened as Chairman, meant to take discussion "further and deeper than fleeting data points or daily market moves." He called the groups an intellectual investment to better equip the Fed "for the next policy conjuncture and beyond," under the theme "One Fed. Fit for Purpose. Focused on the Future." AlphaGen read: the task forces signal a longer-horizon framing alongside meeting-by-meeting data.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Warsh flags AI risks to critical infrastructure, including from "bad actors"
items.take: Chairman Warsh said "great opportunities rarely come risk free," noting that super intelligence "empowers all, including bad actors," and that the Fed is thinking especially of "critical infrastructures and their potential vulnerabilities." He posed open questions on magnitude, scope and timing, including whether total factor productivity will rise and when any surge would start and taper. AlphaGen read: the speech raises questions rather than answers, consistent with his statement that the Fed is "certainly not here to make predictions."
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board

items.headline: Bank of Canada Governor Macklem will not seek a second term; term ends June 2, 2027
items.take: The Bank of Canada said Governor Tiff Macklem told its Board he will not seek a second term when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027. The Board's independent directors have formed a Search Committee, with the process expected to be completed by spring 2027 and the next Governor's seven-year term set to begin June 3, 2027, subject to approval by the Minister of Finance and Cabinet. AlphaGen read: the announcement sets a long runway for a handover at Canada's central bank.
items.source_name: Bank of Canada

items.headline: ECB's Vujčić: euro-area headline inflation rose to 4% in October from 3.8%
items.take: In a Nov. 16 keynote at Euro Finance Week, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić said headline inflation in the euro area increased to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, mainly due to higher energy prices, while underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. He added that weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain inflation by weighing on growth. AlphaGen read: the ECB is describing an energy-driven rise rather than a broad one.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: ECB's Vujčić: US tech capex seen at $5.5 trillion by 2030, AI debt issuance at record
items.take: Vujčić said large cloud and AI infrastructure providers are increasingly turning to debt markets, with issuance volumes reaching record highs this year, and that cumulative capital expenditure by major US technology firms is projected to reach USD 5.5 trillion by 2030. He also said IPO volumes are on track to exceed the dot-com bubble high relative to US GDP. AlphaGen read: the ECB is flagging AI funding as a financial-stability topic, alongside sovereign debt, ahead of its Financial Stability Review two days later.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: ECB's Elderson: about 75% of nationally supervised euro banks are small and non-complex
items.take: In a Nov. 16 contribution for Börsen-Zeitung, ECB Executive Board member Frank Elderson wrote that around 75% of banks supervised by national authorities in the euro area, more than 1,400 institutions, qualify as small and non-complex, with the share at 81% in Germany. Such banks need only report up to 30% of the data reported by larger counterparts. AlphaGen read: the ECB and national supervisors have set out proposals to make oversight of smaller banks more risk-focused without lowering safety standards.
items.source_name: European Central Bank

items.headline: Yuan at 6.6760 per dollar on Nov. 6, from 7.1195 a year earlier
items.take: The Fed's H.10 series on FRED shows 6.6760 Chinese yuan per U.S. dollar on Nov. 6, 2026, versus 7.1195 on Nov. 6, 2025. That is 6.2% fewer yuan per dollar (AlphaGen calculation). AlphaGen read: fewer yuan per dollar means the yuan is worth more in dollar terms than a year ago.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board H.10 via FRED (DEXCHUS)

items.headline: Sterling at $1.3371 on Nov. 6, from $1.3107 a year earlier
items.take: The Fed's H.10 series on FRED shows $1.3371 per British pound on Nov. 6, 2026, versus $1.3107 on Nov. 6, 2025, a rise of 2.0% (AlphaGen calculation). AlphaGen read: the pound buys slightly more dollars than a year ago.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board H.10 via FRED (DEXUSUK)

items.headline: CPI core compounds to about 1.7% over April-October; services 2.0%, goods 0.6%
items.take: Using BLS's published monthly seasonally adjusted changes for April through October 2026, CPI less food and energy compounds to about 1.7%, services less energy services to about 2.0%, and commodities less food and energy commodities to about 0.6% (AlphaGen calculation from rounded figures). AlphaGen read: services have carried most of the core increase over the period.
items.source_name: BLS, Consumer Price Index news release (October 2026)

items.headline: Fed total assets $6.759T on Nov. 11, up $178B from a year earlier
items.take: FRED's WALCL series shows Federal Reserve total assets of $6,758,867M on Nov. 11, 2026, versus $6,580,462M on Nov. 12, 2025, an increase of $178.4B or 2.7% (AlphaGen calculation). AlphaGen read: the balance sheet is larger than a year ago, though it has moved little in recent weeks.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board H.4.1 via FRED (WALCL)

items.headline: Investment-grade spread 0.89 point on Nov. 13, 0.16 above its Jan. 22 low of 0.73
items.take: The ICE BofA US Corporate Index option-adjusted spread was 0.89 percentage point on Nov. 13, per FRED. items.headline: Barr: AI firms' on-balance-sheet debt expected to exceed $800 billion by year-end
items.take: Fed Governor Barr said in Milan on Nov. 16 that on-balance-sheet debt of the seven largest AI firms has been growing significantly in 2026 and is expected to exceed $800 billion before year's end. He cited the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, which estimates the potential maximum nominal value of off-balance-sheet liabilities now exceeds $3 trillion. AlphaGen read: the "potential maximum" wording means the $3 trillion is an upper bound on obligations, not a loss estimate.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech

items.headline: Barr "less concerned about direct losses" from AI boom, flags fire-sale risk
items.take: Governor Barr said that, given the still-limited amount of debt backing the current boom, he is less concerned about direct losses. He added that with leverage at hedge funds and broader risk appetite apparently quite high, a sharp reversal could lead to rapid deleveraging and, potentially, self-reinforcing fire sales. AlphaGen read: his worry is the transmission channel through leveraged holders, not the size of AI debt itself.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech

items.headline: Barr: hyperscalers, GPU makers hold over $100B in equity stakes in LLM labs
items.take: Governor Barr said hyperscaler firms and large GPU producers also have over $100 billion in cumulative equity investments in large language model labs and cloud-computing start-ups. He described this as circular financing, and the speech page says it is a relatively small share of the firms' balance sheets. AlphaGen read: the Fed is flagging the cross-holdings even while describing them as a small share of balance sheets.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech

items.headline: EIA: Flaming Gorge water released to protect Lake Powell power; Hoover Dam exposed
items.take: EIA's Nov. 13 analysis says water was released from Flaming Gorge, in the Upper Colorado River Basin, to reduce the risk of Lake Powell falling below the minimum power pool at Glen Canyon Dam. EIA adds that lower releases from Lake Powell could affect water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. AlphaGen read: the two reservoirs are linked, so protecting one shifts the risk to the other.
items.source_name: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy

items.headline: EIA: El Niño could ease Southwest drought, but one wet year won't erase scarcity
items.take: EIA's Nov. 13 analysis says this year's El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast for the Southwest. EIA cautions, however, that one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. AlphaGen read: the agency's own forecast does not yet count on a rebound, with 2027 Southwest hydropower at 6.1 billion kWh versus 6.13 billion kWh in 2026.
items.source_name: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy

items.headline: EIA: Alaska's Nuna averaging 10,000 b/d this year versus 20,000 b/d expected peak
items.take: EIA's Nov. 12 note says ConocoPhillips' Nuna project, which began production in December 2024, is expected to produce 20,000 barrels per day at its peak and has averaged 10,000 b/d so far this year, partially offsetting existing production declines. By comparison, EIA says the Santos- and Repsol-owned Pikka Phase 1 reached 38,000 b/d as of September 2026. AlphaGen read: Nuna is running at half its stated peak rate, while Pikka's September rate is already above Nuna's peak.
items.source_name: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy

items.headline: EIA: Venezuelan crude to U.S. stopped after Jan. 2019 sanctions; Chevron resumed in 2023
items.take: EIA's Nov. 6 note says U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela stopped shortly after sanctions were imposed on PDVSA in January 2019, and that Chevron resumed exports from its Venezuelan joint venture to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries in January 2023 under waivers granted in November 2022. EIA says the U.S. government eased restrictions on PDVSA following the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and took additional measures to authorize U.S. companies to invest in the country. AlphaGen read: the 701,000 b/d July import figure follows a policy shift, not just refinery demand.
items.source_name: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy

It adds that overall mortgage delinquency rates stayed low on strong home equity cushions, and that delinquencies of Federal Housing Administration loans were above pre-pandemic levels. AlphaGen read: the Fed's picture is of solid aggregate household balance sheets with stress concentrated in auto and FHA loans.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Financial Stability Report (November 2026)

items.headline: Fed stability report: business debt in upper quartile of range

It adds that robust debt issuance by large technology companies may drive aggregate business debt higher over time. AlphaGen read: the report separates healthy large-company credit from a weaker tail.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Financial Stability Report (November 2026)

items.headline: Fed stability report: funding risks moderate, uninsured deposits below 2022 peaks

AlphaGen read: bank funding looks steadier than in 2022 in the Fed's account, with non-bank vehicles the area it flags for continued redemption limits.

items.take: Jefferson said firms and workers will likely broaden and intensify their use of AI and reorganize production and workflows, and that successful firms could gain a competitive advantage, enabling them to expand and draw labor and capital away from competing firms. items.take: Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Nov. 13 at UC San Diego that, in his judgement, the evidence so far 'appears consistent with a contribution to aggregate productivity that is limited, but with the potential to grow quite substantially.' items.take: Citing one recent study, Jefferson said most adopting firms use AI in at most a few business functions, most commonly sales and marketing, strategy and business development, and information technology. AlphaGen read: the speech says it is too early to say what role AI played.

items.headline: Year to date, exports up $297.3B (11.6%) and imports up $204.9B (6.2%)
items.take: BEA and Census say year-to-date exports through September rose $297.3 billion, or 11.6 percent, from the same period in 2025, while imports rose $204.9 billion, or 6.2 percent. The difference, $92.4 billion, matches the reported 12.2 percent drop in the year-to-date goods and services deficit. AlphaGen read: exports have grown faster than imports this year, which is what has narrowed the cumulative deficit.

items.take: For the three months ending September, average exports were up $28.9 billion from the same period a year earlier and average imports were up $65.4 billion. The $36.5 billion difference is the year-over-year widening in the average deficit, which stood at $101.2 billion. AlphaGen read: the three-month view is widening even as the year-to-date total is narrowing, so the comparison period matters.

items.take: BEA reports September exports of services rose $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion, led by a $0.3 billion increase in travel, while imports of services rose $0.8 billion to $79.7 billion, with travel up $0.5 billion and transport up $0.2 billion. items.headline: Fed stability report: hedge fund leverage highest since data began in 2013
items.take: The Fed's November 2026 Financial Stability Report says leverage at hedge funds reached the highest level since the data began in 2013, and that hedge fund gross asset value rose from $4 trillion in 2012 to $13 trillion in 2026. The report generally reflects information available as of Oct. 28, 2026. AlphaGen read: the Fed is flagging leverage outside the banking system as a vulnerability to watch.

items.headline: Fed stability report: bank securities fair value about $330B below book in Q2
items.take: The Fed's November 2026 Financial Stability Report says fair values of banks' available-for-sale and held-to-maturity portfolios were roughly $330 billion below their combined book value in the second quarter of 2026. It adds that yields rising through late October could add further downward pressure. AlphaGen read: higher Treasury yields flow directly into unrealized bank losses.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Financial Stability Report (November 2026)

items.take: The Fed's November 2026 Financial Stability Report says debt issuance tied to advanced computing rose to more than $680 billion by October 2026, with outstanding public debt of more than $1.1 trillion. items.headline: Fed stability report: private credit assets above $2.6T in 2025, defaults at upper end
items.take: The Fed's November 2026 Financial Stability Report says financial assets of private credit vehicles grew from approximately $350 billion in 2012 to more than $2.6 trillion in 2025, and that the loan default rate reached the upper end of its short historical distribution. It says elevated use of payment-in-kind interest indicates some degree of potential repayment difficulties. AlphaGen read: the sector's rapid growth has a short track record.

items.take: The Federal Reserve's November calendar lists Chairman Warsh's opening remarks at a Fed productivity and jobs conference on Monday, Nov. 16 at 12:00 p.m., Governor Waller on payments on Tuesday, Nov. 17 at 9:10 a.m., and Governor Barr on community development on Wednesday, Nov. 18 at 1:35 p.m. Governor Cook is listed Friday, Nov. 20 at 12:15 p.m. AlphaGen read: the productivity theme follows Vice Chair Jefferson's Nov. 13 speech on productivity.

items.headline: Barr: top 10% of households get almost half of U.S. income; top 1% about a fifth
items.take: Fed Governor Barr said the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances, conducted in 2025 and published last month, shows the top 10 percent of households by income receive almost one-half of all income and the top 1 percent about one-fifth. He said inequality is greater for wealth than for income. AlphaGen read: the speech builds the distribution backdrop before turning to how AI may affect it.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech (Nov. 12)

items.headline: Barr: households in the 50th-90th wealth percentiles hold 17% of public stocks by value
items.take: Governor Barr said about three-fourths of households above the median but below the 90th percentile hold stocks, mostly through retirement accounts, yet that group holds only 17 percent of all public stocks by value. He said housing equity has grown more slowly than business equity. AlphaGen read: broader 401(k) ownership has not made stock ownership by value less concentrated, in the Fed's telling.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech (Nov. 12)

items.headline: Barr: bottom half of households hold just over 2% of wealth, an average of $52,000
items.take: Governor Barr said households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution hold just over 2 percent of all wealth, an average of $52,000. He said about 40 percent of them have home equity and nearly 40 percent own business equity, either through a retirement account or their own business, at low values compared with the upper half. AlphaGen read: the speech ties thin balance sheets to a harder time getting by day to day.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech (Nov. 12)

items.headline: Barr: rough estimate puts Forbes 400 wealth share at 4%, up from 3% in 2022
items.take: Governor Barr said that, using Forbes magazine's tally of the 400 wealthiest individuals together with Survey of Consumer Finances data, a rough estimate is that their share of total wealth rose from 3 percent in 2022 to 4 percent in the most recent survey. He added that Forbes counts nearly 1,000 U.S. billionaires. AlphaGen read: Barr labels this a rough estimate, and it sits on top of the survey's finding that concentration rose at the very top.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech (Nov. 12)

items.headline: Barr: labor share held 60-65% after WWII, began falling in 2001, hit 52.8% in Q2
items.take: Governor Barr said the share of national income going to labor was fairly steady between 60 percent and 65 percent after World War II, began falling in fits and starts in 2001, and reached a record low of 52.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026. He said some of the decline reflects measurement issues, but a clear downward trend remains after adjusting for them. AlphaGen read: the Fed is presenting the labor share as a long-run trend that accelerated after the pandemic.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Governor Barr speech (Nov. 12)

items.headline: Jefferson: 40-50% of working adults use AI at work, but few use it daily
items.take: Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said worker surveys find that 40 to 50 percent of working adults use generative AI in their jobs, while only a modest fraction of those users use it every day. He cited the Census Bureau's firm survey showing adoption near 10 percent in mining and in leisure and hospitality, versus roughly 25 percent of all U.S. firms. AlphaGen read: the Fed is describing broad but shallow use, which fits his view that AI's aggregate productivity contribution so far is limited.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Vice Chair Jefferson speech (Nov. 13)

items.headline: Jefferson: one manager survey puts AI gain at 1/2% in sales per employee over three years
items.take: Fed Vice Chair Jefferson cited a recent study of senior managers that estimated AI has boosted sales per employee by just 1/2 percent over the past three years, while other evidence points to substantial efficiency gains on specific tasks. He said most adopting firms use AI in at most a few business functions and noted some firms report AI-generated code contains more errors, requiring more debugging. AlphaGen read: the Fed's own framing is a gap between task-level and firm-level gains.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Vice Chair Jefferson speech (Nov. 13)

items.headline: Jefferson: 32% of workers used computers in 1989; IT lifted 1990s productivity ~3/4 pt
items.take: Fed Vice Chair Jefferson noted that 32 percent of workers used computers at work in 1989, and that investment in information technology capital increased annual labor productivity growth by about 3/4 percentage point in the late 1990s. He said it may be reasonable to apply the same model to AI, a process that takes time to show up in measured productivity. AlphaGen read: the Fed is using the computer era as its template for judging how fast AI could matter.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Vice Chair Jefferson speech (Nov. 13)

Interest is payable each Nov. 13 beginning Nov. 13, 2027, and the notes are senior unsecured obligations ranking equally with the company's other unsecured, unsubordinated debt. items.headline: Jefferson: productivity growth averaged 2.2% in 2020-25, up from 1.5% last cycle
items.take: Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said labor productivity growth averaged 2.2 percent between 2020 and 2025, up from 1.5 percent over the previous business cycle. He noted the pickup began before popular AI chatbots debuted in 2022 and said it is too early to say what role AI played. His judgment is that AI's contribution to aggregate productivity so far appears limited but has the potential to grow quite substantially. AlphaGen read: the Fed's No. 2 official is treating AI as a possible supply-side story rather than a settled one.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Vice Chair Jefferson speech (Nov. 13)

items.headline: CFTC sues Louisiana, its 12th state suit, over event-contract ban
items.take: The CFTC said it sued Louisiana to block the state from prohibiting event contracts offered by CFTC-regulated exchanges, brokers and clearinghouses. The agency said Louisiana obtained a state court order Thursday shutting down more than 30 companies connected to trading of CFTC-regulated derivatives. Louisiana is the 12th state the CFTC has sued, and it has also filed amicus briefs in four federal appeals courts and one state supreme court. AlphaGen read: the jurisdiction fight over prediction markets keeps widening state by state.
items.source_name: CFTC, Release 9326-26

items.headline: Jefferson: ~25% of U.S. firms use AI, near 40% in professional services and information
items.take: In his Nov. 13 speech, Fed Vice Chair Jefferson said surveys find 40 to 50 percent of working adults use generative AI in their jobs, though only a modest fraction use it every day. He said a Census Bureau survey shows roughly 25 percent of all U.S. firms using it in at least one business function, close to 40 percent in knowledge-intensive sectors such as professional services and information, and around 10 percent in mining and in leisure and hospitality. AlphaGen read: adoption is broad among workers but uneven across industries.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Vice Chair Jefferson speech (Nov. 13)

items.headline: Jefferson: IT capital added ~3/4 point to annual productivity growth in late 1990s
items.take: Fed Vice Chair Jefferson said investment in information technology capital raised the annual growth rate of labor productivity by about 3/4 percentage point in the late 1990s. He noted that 32 percent of workers used computers at work in 1989, when national computer spending was barely detectable, a few years after Robert Solow's 1987 remark about the productivity statistics. AlphaGen read: Jefferson uses the computer era to argue that technology's payoff can take years to show up in the data.
items.source_name: Federal Reserve Board, Vice Chair Jefferson speech (Nov. 13)

items.headline: EIA outlook: coal use 419M short tons in 2026, down 7%; 398M in 2027
items.take: EIA's November Short-Term Energy Outlook forecasts U.S. coal consumption of 419 million short tons in 2026, a 7% decrease from 2025, and a further 5% decline in 2027 to 398 million. It expects coal production of 518 million short tons in 2026 and 495 million in 2027, and coal's share of U.S. generation falling from 17% in 2025 to 15% by 2027. AlphaGen read: the forecast has coal use falling in both years as its generation share shrinks.

items.headline: EIA: refiners cut gasoline yield below 45% in 2026 to favor diesel and jet fuel

Distillate yields were above the five-year average in every month, and the fleetwide jet fuel yield has been at or above 12% since March 2026. EIA attributes the shift to distillate and jet margins that are significantly higher because of constrained global supplies.

items.headline: Jefferson to speak tonight on productivity puzzles at UC San Diego roundtable
